subject: Fenwick: VPC storage controls, deletion evidence, and cross-region guarantees
messages:
From: Alex Pruitt <alex.pruitt@fenwickhealth.com>
To: naomi_feldman <naomi.feldman@redwood.ai>
Cc: DataOps Team <dataops@fenwickhealth.com>, Maya Singh <maya.singh@fenwickhealth.com>
Date: 2027-04-20T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Questions: VPC storage controls + proof of deletion

Hi Naomi,

Thanks for the demo yesterday. A few follow-ups from our security and infra teams on the Private (VPC) deployment: we need clear, operational answers for procurement and our security review. Can you confirm the following?

1) When a tenant requests a full-data delete (customer-led exit), what exact artifacts does Redwood produce as proof? We need something we can attach to our compliance folder (timestamps, checksums, snapshot ids, and operator logs are ideal).

2) Does the delete operation remove data from all replication copies and backups (including cross-region replicas and cold snapshots)? If not, what is the retention/retention-exception process?

3) For encrypted customer-controlled storage (we will manage the KMS keys), can Redwood guarantee there are no plaintext copies held by Redwood after delete, and what attestation do you provide?

4) How do you treat short-term object tombstones vs immutable snapshots in terms of availability and proof of erase?

5) We'll need a concise playbook to share with our SOC and vendor-risk teams describing the end-to-end timeline and evidence types for a deletion request.

I attached a requirements spreadsheet (fenwick_requirements.xlsx) with our preferred evidence fields. Appreciate a short on-point response so we can move forward with procurement.

Best,
Alex
Director, Data Engineering
Fenwick Health
(attachment: fenwick_requirements.xlsx - spreadsheet)

From: naomi_feldman <naomi.feldman@redwood.ai>

Cc: karthik_iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>, marissa_cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-04-21T10:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Questions: VPC storage controls + proof of deletion

Alex — thanks for the clear list. High-level answers below; I’m looping in Kar (infra) and Marissa (product/ops) for the technical playbook and artifacts. I’ve attached our current residency matrix and a short deletion playbook draft for your SOC to preview.

Summary answers (short):
- Proof artifacts: deletion job id, UTC timestamps for job start/finish, list of erased object IDs/paths, snapshot ids retired, operator audit log excerpt (sha256), and automated verification report (checksums where applicable).
- Cross-region and backups: we run a coordinated cascade delete. Active replicas and warm snapshots are included; cold snapshots and long-term backups depend on your configured snapshot retention policy and whether you manage keys (if you revoke keys for customer-managed KMS, data becomes unrecoverable).
- Customer-managed KMS: when you control the key, Redwood does not hold unencrypted copies of your data. We provide an attestation statement and a key-operation log extract showing key revocation/rotate timestamps.
- Tombstones vs snapshots: tombstones are ephemeral delete markers; they are processed into background compaction that reclaims storage. Immutable snapshots are explicit retention points and require separate retirement; our evidence will call out which snapshots were retired.

Next steps: Kar will send the technical sequence with exact log fields and verification commands; Marissa will map timing expectations for each phase (immediate delete job, replication sweep, snapshot retirement, final verification).

Thanks — Naomi
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
(attachment: residency_matrix_v2.pdf; attachment: vpc_deletion_playbook_v1.docx)

From: karthik_iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>

Cc: marissa_cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-04-22T11:47:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Questions: VPC storage controls + proof of deletion

Alex — following up with the technical sequence you can include in the procurement packet. I kept this practical and field-level so your infra team can validate.

Operational deletion sequence (ordered):
1) Customer requests deletion via API or Console -> system returns deletion_job_id (UUID) and enqueues job.
2) Immediate soft-delete phase: object metadata marked with tombstone; tombstone timestamped (UTC) and audit entry created with operator and system service ids.
3) Replication sweep: orchestrator sends delete to all active replica shards. Each replica returns a replica_ack record correlated to deletion_job_id. Replica acknowledgements include node id, region, and per-object checksum if object-store-level checksums are enabled.
4) Snapshot retirement: explicit snapshots referencing the tenant are listed. For each snapshot scheduled for retirement we emit snapshot_retire_event with snapshot_id, retained_until (if a retention policy prevented immediate retirement), and when retired, retired_at timestamp and retiring_operator id.
5) Background reclamation: garbage collector compacts tombstones into storage reclamation — this step reclaims blocks and writes a reclamation_manifest listing reclaimed block ids; manifest checksum is provided.
6) Cold backups: if you manage KMS keys and you rotate/revoke the key for the tenant, any backups encrypted with that key become cryptographically inaccessible — we provide the key-operation log (kms_action_id, action, timestamp). If Redwood manages keys, we will list the backup objects and their retention state; we can schedule an expedited purge under addendum.

Evidence artifacts produced automatically or on-demand:
- deletion_job_id (UUID)
- deletion_job_start and deletion_job_end (ISO UTC)
- list of object IDs / storage paths (plain text list)
- replica_ack_log.csv (node_id, region, object_count, checksum_flag)
- snapshot_retire_manifest.json (snapshot_id, retired_at)
- reclamation_manifest.tar.gz (list of block ids and checksum)
- operator_audit_excerpt.txt (sha256 of log excerpt)
- verification_report.html (automated read-verify run)

How we prove cross-region coverage: each replica_ack entry is cryptographically signed by the node's signing key. We make the signing public key part of the attestation package (attestation_manifest.pem). You can validate that every active region returned an ack for the deletion_job_id.

Key management notes:
- Customer-managed KMS: best for cryptographic guarantees. Revoking/rotating the key is accepted as acceptable proof of irrecoverability; we include the KMS action records.
- Redwood-managed KMS: we can provide object lists and retention schedules and perform deletes; for cold archival snapshots we will need an SLA addendum for expedited removal.

Timing expectations: typical timeline for a full-coverage delete (no long-term retention exceptions, customer-managed KMS) is 24–72 hours for active replica sweep + snapshot retirements; final reclamation may be queued behind compaction windows (configurable). We'll include a timeline matrix in the playbook.

Attachment: key_rotation_kms_diagram.png (diagram showing KMS flow).

Let us know which artifacts your auditors require verbatim and we can produce a tailored evidence bundle (machine-readable CSV/JSON + signed manifest).

— Kar
Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference

Naomi / Kar — this is helpful, thank you. A few quick clarifications so my SOC can close the item:

• For the evidence bundle we requested: can you include the signed attestation_manifest.pem and a machine-readable replica_ack_log.csv? Our auditors want to be able to run a simple validation script against those files.
• For cold backups: Fenwick will manage the KMS key. Can you confirm the timeline if we revoke the KMS key immediately upon delete request? Is that the same 24–72 hour window or faster for cryptographic irrecoverability?
• Finally, can you add a short blurb to the playbook that describes operator access controls during a delete event (who can trigger, who can approve, how approvals are logged)? Our legal team likes those named roles.

If you can drop an updated deletion playbook and a sample evidence bundle (redacted) by EOD Wednesday we can include it in our vendor-risk signoff.

Appreciate it — Alex
Director, Data Engineering, Fenwick Health
